content: 1. Displays that are either served by vessel staff or are self-service are included in this context. 2. Food-handling areas are defined as any location where food is stored, processed, prepared, or served. 3. Food preparation areas specifically refer to locations where food is processed, cooked, or prepared for service. 4. Food service areas are any locations where food is presented to passengers or crew members, excluding individual cabin service. 5. Food storage areas are defined as any location where food or food products are stored. 6. Food transportation corridors are areas primarily intended for moving food during preparation, storage, and service operations, such as service lift vestibules, provision corridors, and corridors connecting preparation and service areas. 7. Corridors used exclusively for transporting closed beverages and packaged foods (e.g., bottled/canned beverages, crackers, chips) are not considered food transportation corridors, but the deck/bulkhead junction must be coved. 8. Excluded areas include passenger and crew corridors, public areas, individual cabin service, dining rooms connected to galleys, and food loading areas used solely for food delivery to the vessel. 9. A food waste system is a system designed to collect, transport, and process food waste from food areas to a waste disposal system, such as a pulper or vacuum system. 10. A gap is defined as an open junction exceeding 3 millimeters (1/8 inch). 11. A gravity drain is a fitting used to drain water from a recreational water facility by gravity without any downstream pump. 12. A gravity drainage system is a water collection system where a collection tank is located between the recreational water facility and the suction pumps. 13. Gray water refers to wastewater from galley equipment, deck drains, dishwashers, showers, baths, laundries, washbasins, and recirculated recreational water facilities. It does not include black water or bilge water from machinery spaces. 14. A gutterway is synonymous with a scupper, which channels liquid runoff to a deck drain. 15. Halogens, such as chlorine, bromine, and iodine, are elements used for water disinfection. 16. A health hazard is any impairment that poses an actual risk to public health, such as poisoning or the spread of disease through contaminated water, sewage, industrial fluids, or waste. 17. A hose bib connection vacuum breaker (HVB) is a backflow prevention device that attaches directly to a hose bib via a threaded head. It includes a single check valve and vacuum breaker vent and is specifically designed for hose connections.g., when a shut-off valve is located downstream). 18. An interactive recreational water facility is an indoor or outdoor facility with features like misting, jetting, waterfalls, or sprinkling that involve water recirculation systems in contact with bathers. Additional features, such as decorations or fountains connected to the recirculation system, also classify the facility as interactive. These facilities may have zero depth, and enclosed water slides are considered interactive recreational water facilities. 19. Keel laying refers to the date when construction identifiable with a specific ship begins, and when at least 50 tons or 1% of the ship's estimated structural mass (whichever is less) has been assembled. 20. mg/L (milligrams per liter) is the metric equivalent of parts per million (ppm). 21. 22. Nonfood-contact surfaces (nonfood zones) include all exposed surfaces of equipment in food areas that are not food-contact surfaces. 23. Permeate water lines are pipes carrying permeate water from the reverse osmosis unit, which may be directed to the potable water system. 24. pH (potential hydrogen) is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, measuring the acidity or alkalinity of a solution. Values between 0 and 7 indicate acidity, while values between 7 and 14 indicate alkalinity. Pure distilled water has a neutral pH of 7. 25. A plumbing fixture is a receptacle or device that is either permanently or temporarily connected to the vessel's water distribution system and demands a water supply or discharges used water, waste materials, or sewage to the drainage system. 26. Portable equipment is readily removable, mounted on casters, gliders, or rollers, or equipped with a mechanical means for safe tilting during cleaning. It can be moved easily by one person. 27. 28. Readily accessible means exposed or capable of being exposed for cleaning or inspection without the use of tools. 29. Readily removable refers to the ability to detach a component from the main unit without using tools. 30. Recreational seawater is seawater taken onboard while the vessel is underway at least 12 miles at sea and routed directly to recreational water facilities for sea-to-sea exchange or recirculation. 31. A recreational water facility (RWF) is a water facility modified, improved, constructed, or installed for public swimming or recreational bathing. Examples include activity pools, baby-only water facilities, children’s pools, diving pools, hot tubs, hydrotherapy pools, interactive recreational water facilities, slides, spa pools, swimming pools, therapeutic pools, wading pools, and whirlpools. 32. 33. Removable components can be detached from the main unit using simple tools like a screwdriver, pliers, or an open-end wrench. 34. A safety vacuum release system (SVRS) is designed to release a vacuum at a suction outlet caused by high vacuum due to a blockage in the outlet flow. These systems must comply with ASTM F2387-04 or ANSI/ASME A112.19.17-2002 standards. 35. Sanitary seawater lines are water lines carrying seawater intended for use in potable water production systems or recreational water facilities. 36. A scupper is a conduit or collection basin that channels liquid runoff to a deck drain. 37. Sealant is a material used to fill seams. 38. A seam is an open junction greater than 0.8 millimeters (1/32 inch) but less than 3 millimeters (1/8 inch). 39. A smooth food-contact surface is free of pits and inclusions, with cleanability equal to or exceeding that of 100-grit number 3 stainless steel. Nonfood-contact surfaces of equipment must also meet specific smoothness standards.
